messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Hey! No HPR cert needed for this one. I have a G54. Make it fly as high as is sensible, but it must come down under 6 m/s. Single stage only. It usually blows around 10 mph at our field.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: motor is fixed, a G54. No high-power certification, so the motor must stay at G or below, which a G54 does if the catalog agrees. Fly as high as is sensible: light airframe, small diameter, still stable. Landing is a maximum of 6 m/s. Single stage (fixed). Wind is about 10 mph: 10 * 0.447 = 4.47 m/s, and I will pass that on every flight. Rail is not stated, so 1.5 m. Vertical, sea level.
2. Feasibility: a sensible G flight is a few hundred metres, not a minimum-diameter dart that weathercocks in a 4.47 m/s breeze. I need the G54's impulse, diameter and delays before sizing.

2. Feasibility: G54 resolves to the AeroTech G54W, class G, 81.1 N*s, 56.3 N average, burn 1.44 s, 29 mm. That is under the high-power line. Delays are 6, 10 and 14 s. 81 N*s will not make a heavy rocket climb, so the sensible altitude build is a light 41 mm cardboard tube, stable but not over-finned, because 4.47 m/s of wind will weathercock a very stable rocket.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.25 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 56.3 / (0.25 * 9.81) = 23.0. Rail acceleration (56.3 - 2.45) / 0.25 = 215 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 215 * 1.5) = 25.4 m/s. Descent mass 0.25 - 0.046 = 0.204 kg. At 5 m/s and Cd 0.8, area = 2 * 0.204 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.163 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.163 / 3.1416) = 0.456 m. A 0.55 m chute stays under 6 m/s without hanging in the wind forever. Burnout at 1.44 s and a coast of roughly 8 s fits the 10 s delay better than the 6 s one.
4. Draft: 41 mm cardboard, 0.48 m long, polystyrene ogive, three balsa fins of modest span, 29 mm mount, G54W-10, 0.55 m chute on ejection. Wind 4.47 m/s, rail 1.5 m.

4. Check: the simulator gives a static margin of -0.07 cal at rail exit, and -0.07 cal through the burn. That fails both the 1 cal launch gate and the requirement to stay positive during the burn. The rocket is unstable, so the 808.2 m apogee is not a flight I can keep. Landing 3.8 m/s is under 6, rail exit 30.4 m/s and thrust-to-weight 26.5 would have passed. Liftoff mass is 0.217 kg, a bit under my 0.25 kg guess, which put the CG even farther back on the G54W. The modest fins were too small.
5. Fix: -0.07 cal is the failing value. Fin area was (0.08 + 0.03) / 2 * 0.055 = 0.0030 m^2. New fins are root 0.13 m, tip 0.045 m, span 0.10 m, sweep 0.06 m, area (0.13 + 0.045) / 2 * 0.10 = 0.0088 m^2, and 0.0088 / 0.0030 = 2.9 times the area. That is a normal sport fin for a 41 mm tube, large enough to get the CP behind the motor without turning it into a weathercock. Tube, nose, motor and chute stay the same.

4. Check: the simulator gives 0.6 cal at rail exit and 0.6 cal through the burn. The burn stays positive, but 0.6 is still under the 1.0 cal launch gate. Apogee came down to 679.3 m once the rocket was no longer flying backwards, which is a sensible height for 81 N*s. Landing 3.9 m/s, rail exit 30.8 m/s, thrust-to-weight 25.5. The larger fins were not enough on their own because the G54W is more than half the mass and it sits on the tail.
5. Fix: 0.6 cal still fails. More fin would make a 41 mm rocket look like a kite in a 4.47 m/s wind, so the CG has to come forward. Adding 0.04 kg of nose weight at the top of the tube. That is 0.04 / 0.225 = 0.18 of liftoff mass, ahead of the motor. Fins, airframe and the G54W-10 stay as they are.

4. Check: the simulator gives 1.75 cal at rail exit and 1.75 cal through the burn, above 1.0. Apogee is 702.6 m. That is actually higher than the unstable-fin case: 702.6 - 679.3 = 23.3 m, because it stopped weathercocking in the 4.47 m/s wind. Landing is 4.3 m/s, under 6. Rail exit 27.7 m/s, thrust-to-weight 21.6. The chute opens at 11.5 s, which is 11.5 - 9.66 = 1.8 s after apogee, and it still lands softly. Motor is the class-G G54W, so no high-power certification is required.
5. Fix: no further change; margin and landing both pass.
6. Uncertainty: 702 m is as high as this light cardboard rocket goes while staying stable in a 4.47 m/s wind. OpenRocket's drag and the real balsa mass will move that. The chute opens 1.8 s late at 17.6 m/s, so the shock is firmer than an apogee opening; the 10 s delay is a bit long, but shortening it would open the canopy while the rocket is still climbing and give away altitude. Drift was 647 m, which is a real field requirement at 10 mph. The 0.04 kg nose weight is what holds the 1.75 cal margin.
messages.content:
A light 41 mm cardboard rocket on an AeroTech G54W-10, with 0.04 kg of nose weight and a 0.55 m chute.
In a 4.47 m/s wind the simulator gives 703 m, 1.75 cal of margin, 27.7 m/s off the rail, and a 4.3 m/s landing.
